name: AnyEdit
tagline: Browser-based editors for PSD, PDF, DOCX and XLSX that process files locally instead of uploading them.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The architecture here is not the hard part: everything runs client side, so an agent can scaffold a local-only editor in an afternoon using pdf-lib, pdf.js, SheetJS, mammoth and ag-psd. What you cannot one-shot is fidelity. PSD smart objects, layer effects and blend modes, DOCX styles surviving a round trip, XLSX formulas and charts coming back intact, these are years of edge-case grinding against formats that were never meant to be reimplemented. A DIY build will open, inspect and lightly modify files just fine, and will quietly mangle anything complicated. If your actual need is crop a PSD layer, fill a PDF form, tweak a spreadsheet, build it. If you hand clients the output, don't.
coreLoopDIY: A local web app that opens PSD, PDF, DOCX and XLSX entirely in the browser, lets you view, lightly edit and re-export each, with no upload step.
requirements: No server, no accounts, no API keys
Open source format libraries: pdf-lib, pdf.js, SheetJS, mammoth, docx, ag-psd
Patience with files that round trip badly
whatYouLose: Round-trip fidelity: DOCX styles, XLSX formulas and charts, PSD layer effects will degrade or vanish
PSD features beyond flat layer compositing: smart objects, adjustment layers, blend mode accuracy
Real PDF text editing with reflow, plus OCR on scanned pages
A consistent, tested UI across four very different format editors instead of four half-finished panels
Ongoing fixes when a file from some app version parses weird, which is most of the actual work
moatNotes: The moat is not the client-side trick, that is just a build flag. It is the thousands of malformed real-world files already fixed.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the value is that the file comes out the other side unbroken, and that is almost entirely accumulated bug fixes. Anyone can render a PSD preview; very few can save one that Photoshop reopens without complaint. People also pay for the convenience of one tab that handles whatever a colleague emailed them, without installing Office, Acrobat and Photoshop, and without trusting an upload. A local build matches the privacy story exactly and the correctness story not at all.
notes: Client-side is the easy half of this product. The hard half is every file ever exported by a weird plugin.
prompt:
Build a local-only, browser-based multi-format file editor. No backend, no accounts, no telemetry, no uploads: every file is parsed and written in the browser.

Stack, non-negotiable: Vite + React + TypeScript + Tailwind. Single page app, static build, runs from `npm run dev` and `npm run preview`. No server routes at all.

Layout: a drag-and-drop dropzone. Sniff the file by extension and magic bytes, then route to one of four editor panels.

PDF panel: render pages with pdf.js into a canvas list. Support page reorder, page delete, page rotate, and filling AcroForm text fields. Write the result with pdf-lib and download it. No text reflow editing, state that clearly in the UI.

XLSX panel: parse with SheetJS. Show a sheet tab bar and an editable grid of cell values. Support editing raw cell values and adding or deleting rows and columns. Re-export with SheetJS. Warn in the UI that formulas, charts and conditional formatting may not survive a round trip.

DOCX panel: render a read-only preview with mammoth to HTML. Allow find-and-replace across the document text and rebuild a simplified .docx with the `docx` library. Be explicit in the UI that this is a simplified rebuild and complex styling is lost.

PSD panel: parse with ag-psd. Show the layer tree with per-layer visibility toggles and opacity, render a composite preview to canvas, and export flattened PNG plus a re-saved PSD. Smart objects, adjustment layers and layer effects are out of scope; grey them out with a tooltip.

Cross-cutting: run parsing in a Web Worker so the UI does not freeze on large files. Show file size, format and a dry one-line capability note per panel. All downloads via Blob and object URLs.

Write a README that lists, per format, exactly what is supported and what is known to break. Do not overpromise in copy. Do not add cloud storage pickers, sign-in, or analytics. Include a .env.example only if you genuinely need a variable, otherwise omit it.
